name: Almoravid dynasty
summary: A Berber religious movement from the Sahara that founded Marrakesh (1070), ruled Morocco and Muslim Spain, and defeated Castile at Sagrajas (1086), until the Almohads overthrew it.

knownFor.label: Almoravid dinar
knownFor.note: Gold coin used across the Mediterranean.

location.value: Present-day Morocco and Mauritania, the western Maghreb and al-Andalus (Muslim Iberia).

terrain.value: Saharan desert, Atlas mountains, Moroccan plains and Andalusian valleys.

climate.value: Desert in the south, Mediterranean in the north.

resources.value: Gold from Ghana and West Africa.

urbanisation.value: Marrakesh (founded about 1070) was the capital; other major cities included Fez, Seville and Córdoba.

disease.value: Plague outbreaks, above all the Black Death (1347–51).

migration.value: Sanhaja Berber tribes from the Sahara moved north into the Maghreb and al-Andalus.

economicBase.value: Control of the trans-Saharan trade routes and West African gold, plus Islamic taxes and the spoils of conquest.

tradeRoutes.value: Trans-Saharan routes to Ghana and about 18 major ports on both sides of the Strait of Gibraltar.

wealth.value: Wealthy in its early years, minting more gold than ever before.

moneyAndTax.value: Promised to collect only taxes allowed by Islamic law, but these were not enough to pay for its armies.

inequality.value: Berber warrior elite over Andalusians and farmers.

governmentType.value: Its rulers took the title Amir al-Muslimin and formally accepted the Abbasid caliphs in Baghdad as overlords.

keyRulers.value: Abdallah ibn Yasin (religious leader). Abu Bakr ibn Umar. Yusuf ibn Tashfin (died 1106). Ali ibn Yusuf (1106–1143).

institutions.value: Maliki jurists (fuqaha) strongly supported the dynasty.

stability.value: Strong under Yusuf ibn Tashfin; weakened by Christian advances and the Almohad rebellion from the 1120s.

eliteConflict.value: Rivalries inside the ruling family, such as Abu Bakr's son Ibrahim against Yusuf ibn Tashfin.

armyAndTech.value: Infantry with javelins and pikes in a phalanx, supported by camel riders and horsemen; a navy to cross the Strait of Gibraltar.

majorWars.value: Battle of Sagrajas (1086), defeating Alfonso VI of Castile and León; the Almohad rebellion from the 1120s.

territoryChange.value: From 1090 took direct control of the taifa kingdoms; by 1106 it held all of al-Andalus except Zaragoza.

alliancesRivals.value: Fought Castile and Aragon; overthrew the taifa kingdoms.

openness.value: Open to trade; closed to rival faiths at times.

communicationTransport.value: Trans-Saharan trade routes and a navy that ferried troops across the Strait of Gibraltar.

artsArchitecture.value: The Almoravid Qubba in Marrakesh and the Great Mosque of Tlemcen.

socialStructure.value: Veiled Sanhaja Berber rulers from the Sahara over Andalusi and Maghrebi townspeople and farmers.

sharedIdentity.value: A shared reformist, strict Maliki Sunni Islam.

dailyLife.value: Village farming; bread, porridge and beer or wine.

neighbours.value: Ghana Empire, Castile and León, Aragon.

riseSignals.value: The reform movement that Abdallah ibn Yasin preached to the Sanhaja Berbers in the 1040s.

peakPeriod.value: By Yusuf ibn Tashfin's death in 1106 it held all of al-Andalus except Zaragoza.

declineSignals.value: Christian advances, an uprising in Córdoba (1121) and the Almohad rebellion started by Ibn Tumart in the 1120s.

overallCertainty.value: Main events are known from chronicles and charters; population figures are estimates.
